opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when we were training them, I didn't treat the shared architecture as something already proven. It was more of a hypothesis we kept testing.

The logic behind sharing one architecture is simple. If the design is right, it should hold across scales. The smaller model, Flash, lets you iterate quickly and cheaply. You can run many ablations, find problems early, and see how the training dynamics behave. Then you carry that understanding to the larger model. If you used two different architectures, every lesson from the small one would carry an asterisk, and you'd lose much of that leverage.

But I was always a bit wary of over-trusting the small-scale results. Some things look fine at small scale and only show their problems when you scale up: training stability, loss spikes, how the attention or routing behaves with longer context, how the efficiency trade-offs change. So during Pro's training we watched closely for any sign that the architecture was breaking down in ways Flash hadn't shown us.

What gave me more confidence over time was consistency. The scaling behavior matched our expectations, the stability issues we'd anticipated were manageable, and the capability gains looked like what you'd hope for from more parameters and compute, not something odd caused by the architecture. That consistency between the two models was the strongest evidence that the design was sound.

That said, I wouldn't call any architecture final. Every training run teaches you something, and some of what we learned from these models will definitely shape what we change next. Being sound for this generation is different from being the right answer forever.

fable-5.1.text:
When we started V2, the first decision we made was that Flash and Pro would not be two separate research lines. They share one architecture, and the only thing that really changes is scale. I was fairly confident about the soundness of that from the start, but confidence in the architecture and confidence that it will hold at a different size are two different things, so we were quite disciplined about testing it.

The way I think about it is that an architecture is only "sound" if the decisions inside it survive scaling. A lot of choices look great at a few billion parameters and then quietly stop mattering, or start hurting, when you go up. So before committing Pro, we ran a scaling ladder on the Flash design. We looked at whether the MoE routing stayed balanced, whether the attention changes we made for long context kept their efficiency advantage without losing quality, and whether the loss curve extrapolated in a way we trusted. If something only helped at small scale, we removed it even if the small-scale number looked nice. That filtering is what made me comfortable calling the design sound.

Flash was also our proving ground in a very practical sense. Training a smaller model first means you catch the mistakes cheaply. We found several things on Flash, around training stability and around how the model behaved after a couple of trillion tokens, that we fixed before Pro consumed any serious compute. So Flash gave us the empirical evidence, and Pro was the bet that the evidence generalized.

I will say honestly that there were moments of doubt. Pro is expensive enough that you do not get many retries, and when a curve wobbled midway through, there is always a voice asking whether the architecture is the problem. Every time, when we traced it, it came down to data or optimization details rather than the structure itself. That actually strengthened my view. The architecture kept behaving the way the smaller model predicted, and that predictability is, to me, the strongest sign that the design was right.

The other reason I liked a shared design is engineering. One kernel stack, one inference path, one set of tooling. Anything we optimize for Flash transfers straight to Pro, and the behaviors users learn on one model carry over to the other. That matters more than people think when you are a relatively small team competing with much larger ones.

astra-6.text: I’d separate two questions: whether the shared architecture was sound, and whether it was the best fit for both Flash and Pro. Sharing an architecture doesn’t, by itself, establish either. During training, I’d look for stable optimization, consistent improvements as compute increased, and whether those improvements carried through to evaluation. If both models showed that pattern, it would give me confidence in the foundation. But I’d still assess their trade-offs separately—a design that works well for Pro may not be the most efficient choice for Flash.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the key question was whether the architecture would behave consistently as we scaled training. A design can look very convincing on paper, but you still have to see whether optimization remains stable and whether improvements carry through to actual capabilities.

Sharing an architecture between Flash and Pro gives you a useful way to examine that. But I wouldn’t take success with one as proof that everything is right with the other. They have different efficiency and capability goals, so you still need to validate each model. My confidence would come from that repeated experimental feedback, rather than from the elegance of the architecture alone.
